title: Playing duets and recording with Oliver; advice to young trumpeters
summary: He recalls the Oliver duets, first recordings around 1922, adapting to the mic, then advice about lip care and young players who will not learn.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Well, I stayed with Oliver a long time. See what I mean? After I stayed with Oliver, we got so wedged in together making duets and musicians like Bix and Paul Whiteburn and all them people sitting down. They couldn't understand how we played so well together. When Joe got ready for a break, I had every note to it. And we just sitting right there and didn't say nothing to each other. That's how well I loved them. When did you start recording? When was the first? With Joe Oliver. About 1922. The same time of the New Orleans Rhythm Kings was recording down in Richmond, Indiana for the, what is that, the Ginette record. Now most of Joe's tunes are on the Ginette. And I was a young country boy there, you know, and there were quite nice Joe's fading out. And in those early days, the musicians didn't take care of their teeth and the days of powery, you know, all that number. Well, that was Joe's downfall. Well, quite naturally, he could take his teeth. You couldn't do that. Now I'd play trumpet the way you have to play. See? Well, quite naturally, if I'm going to play second trumpet, I had to get to the door. And we had them horns. They didn't have mics. Joe had to get right up in the mic. Lean right into it. Yeah, because his tone didn't register like Bob Johnson's did. See? And with my tone and strong, I had to get there in order to blend with Joe's. I showed you how to time. I said, now you can stand anywhere and play. You got a mic to catch it. Do you suppose it's easier now for a kid under comparable situations? Much easier. If he'd just gone and take out the idea that if we try to show him something, you know, they'll tell you, well, you're an old man. Yeah. But they ain't thinking about the strategy and as you age up, you know, they're a little kid in my neighborhood. He was so outstanding on bugle in school, you know, neighbor. And I said, well, I'll write and give him a trumpet, which I did. And bought a little method. We had little duets and things. And every time I go to say, now, you see this phrase here. He said, oh, I know that. You know what I mean? Well, I'm a busy man. You know, I ain't got too much time. I already know what he's doing. So I said, now, you just take him on, you know, and enjoy yourself. Because I ain't got time to try to teach somebody that already knew everything. And that's the kids for you nowadays. Do you find that everywhere you go? Well, I don't bother about it. I ain't no teacher. They ask me a question. I keep my lips up and everything. I say, well, a little witch hazel. Never try to jive them and lip salves that we get from Germany. The musician's been buying all the time. It's just guys don't want to be bought because it's greasy or something. But it penetrates and keeps the lips strong. And you have a person. See, one thing I told the youngsters. Okay, great. Your knowledge is I'm a trumpet. You can be a voice to your soul or whatever it is. But if your emphasis is not strong to exercise what you got in mind, you're in trouble. Same as a fighter. If he knock your block off, he get to you. But if them legs don't get him out the way of a punch, what good is it?
